query: Reported superconducting high-entropy alloys are dominated by Nb-Ta matrices, while other studies concern titanium-rich systems based on heavy transition metals and partly ordered systems. Consequently, these precedents do not establish what controls superconductivity in high-entropy alloys outside the best-studied material classes. Within the defining constraint of a solid solution containing at least five elements at no less than 5 atomic percent each, what governs superconducting behavior in such an uncharacterized high-entropy alloy, and why? State one testable mechanistic hypothesis, a controlled comparison against the starting material, predicted observations relative to the baseline, applicable boundary conditions, the earlier evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In a single‐phase high-entropy alloy solid solution (with ≥5 elements at ≥5 at.% each) that is not based on the well-studied Nb–Ta or Ti-rich heavy transition metal systems, the superconducting transition temperature is mainly governed by the degree of lattice distortion induced by atomic size mismatch. This distortion alters the phonon spectrum and electron–phonon coupling strength, which in turn shifts Tc.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, disordered single-phase high-entropy alloy composed of at least five constituent elements (each present at no less than 5 at.%), prepared outside the typical Nb–Ta or Ti-rich heavy metal classes.
generation.intervention: Perform a controlled compositional modification by substituting one constituent element with another that has a similar electronic character but a significantly larger atomic radius. This change increases the overall lattice distortion without a large alteration in the average valence electron count.
generation.conditions: Both the baseline and modified alloys are synthesized using identical processing routes (e.g., arc-melting followed by identical annealing treatments) to achieve a single-phase solid solution. Their superconducting properties are measured under identical conditions (ambient pressure, temperatures spanning below and above the expected Tc, using resistivity and magnetic susceptibility measurements).
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced lattice distortion (local strain fields) resulting from increased atomic size mismatch.
generation.mechanism: The increased lattice distortion modifies the phonon density of states and strengthens the electron–phonon interaction, thereby altering the density of states at the Fermi level and shifting the superconducting transition temperature.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline alloy, the modified alloy (with enhanced lattice distortion) will show a measurable shift in Tc (either an increase or decrease, with the magnitude dependent on the extent of the distortion) when measured by low-temperature resistivity and susceptibility tests.
generation.baseline: The unmodified high-entropy alloy solid solution (with the original set of elements and uniform single-phase structure) whose superconducting transition temperature has been established under the same processing and measurement conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies only to disordered, single-phase solid solution HEAs (each element ≥5 at.%) synthesized under similar conditions; it does not extend to multiphase or partially ordered alloys or to alloys dominated by the Nb–Ta or Ti-rich heavy transition metal matrices.
generation.uncertainty: While the mechanism posits that increased lattice distortion alters electron–phonon coupling to shift Tc, the exact direction and magnitude of the change in Tc is uncertain without detailed calculations and may depend on subtle details of the phonon spectrum and density of states.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two alloy batches: (1) the baseline high-entropy alloy and (2) an alloy with a controlled substitution that increases lattice distortion. Confirm phase homogeneity and quantify lattice parameters via X-ray diffraction. Then, measure the superconducting transition temperatures using resistivity and magnetic susceptibility at identical temperatures and pressures.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (to assess lattice parameters and strain)
Four-probe electrical resistance as a function of temperature (to determine Tc)
Magnetic susceptibility measurements (to confirm bulk superconductivity)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloy with enhanced lattice distortion does not exhibit a statistically significant alteration in Tc relative to the baseline (after excluding effects from phase separation or inhomogeneity), then the hypothesis that lattice distortion governs superconductivity is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In 2014, the first superconducting high-entropy alloy Ta0.34Nb0.33Hf0.08Zr0.14Ti0.11 (in at.%) was discovered []. According to Sun and Cava [], this alloy can be classified as a type-A HEA superconductor. HEAs of this type contain only metals on the left side of the transition metal region of the periodic table, crystallize in a body-centered cubic (bcc) lattice, and exhibit superconducting transition temperatures (Tc) between 4.0 and 9.2 K, while their highest upper critical field (μ0Hc2) is close to 12 T [,,,,,,]. These are the most widely studied HEA superconductors to date. However, it should be noted that most of these alloys contain a large amount of niobium and tantalum, while the titanium concentration is typically less than 20 at.%. Because binary Nb-Ti alloys exhibit much better superconducting properties than Nb-Ta [], it is plausible to expect that NbTi-based high-entropy alloys will have a higher Tc and/or μ0Hc2 compared to previously reported type-A HEA superconductors. Pressure is one of the variables that can uncover unexpected phenomena and properties (). For superconductors in particular, the pressure-induced enhancement of critical transition temperatures in copper-oxide and iron-pnictide superconductors (), the reemergence of superconductivity in the alkaline iron selenide () and heavy fermion superconductors (), pressure-induced superconductivity in H3S () and elements (, ), are examples. Therefore, looking for new phenomena in the superconducting HEA under pressure is of great interest. Here we report high-pressure studies on the superconducting HEA (TaNb)0.67(HfZrTi)0.33, which has a critical transition temperature to the superconducting state (TC) of about 7.8 K at ambient pressure (, ). Our observations demonstrate that this alloy exhibits extraordinarily robust superconductivity––its zero-resistance superconducting state is still achieved even at a pressure of 190.6 GPa, or almost 2 megabars (1 Mbar = 1011 pascal), a pressure like that within the outer core of the earth. Such a superconductor with a highly robust zero-resistance state, existing continuously from 1 atm to geological pressures, is extremely unusual and is in fact unique
